Inscrições abertas para Programa de Voluntariado no HEJ Estão abertas as inscrições para o Programa de Voluntariado para atuação no Hospital Estadual de Jataí Dr. Serafim de Carvalho (HEJ). A iniciativa é realizada em parceria com a Organização das Voluntárias de Goiás (OVG) e visa selecionar pessoas interessadas em atuar em atividades de acolhimento, humanização e apoio dentro da unidade hospitalar. As vagas disponíveis são para as funções de Músico(a), Doula, Posso Ajudar, Animador(a), Instrutor(a) de Artesanato, Apoio Espiritual e Apoio Operacional. Os interessados precisam participar do treinamento online "Voluntários do Bem", que será realizado nesta quinta-feira, dia 22 de outubro, das 15h às 16h30, e vai abordar os benefícios da atuação solidária, os aspectos éticos e legais e como ingressar na OVG ou em instituições parceiras. O cadastro é feito pela Plataforma do Voluntariado, por meio do QR Code disponível na arte, e a capacitação acontece pelo link: https://www.ovg.org.br/voluntariado/capacitacao/

Pessoal, quero apresentar uma oportunidade para as empresas que desejam desenvolver suas equipes comerciais. O Instituto Leão oferece o Treinamento de Vendas e Resultados, um programa estruturado em 8 módulos, com 4 horas de duração cada, totalizando quase 40 horas de desenvolvimento comercial por meio de workshops práticos e experiências vivenciais. Ao longo do programa, trabalhamos comunicação, escuta, negociação, relacionamento com clientes, fechamento de vendas e desenvolvimento do comportamento comercial. A proposta vai além de transmitir conteúdo. É colocar as pessoas em situações práticas, provocar reflexão e transformar o aprendizado em ações que contribuam para os resultados da equipe. Para as empresas que desejam investir nesse desenvolvimento, preparei uma condição comercial especial para a primeira empresa que formalizar a contratação do programa completo, válida até o dia 20 de outubro. Se você é empresário ou gestor e quer entender como esse trabalho pode ser aplicado à realidade da sua equipe, me chama no particular. Do **not** reach for this when refs work fine — `browser_click` / `browser_type` on a stable `@eN` ref is simpler and self-documenting. Use this when refs are unstable, expensive, or the element is unreachable by scoping. ### Hermes PhotoCraft / canvas control order For PhotoCraft, keep owner and interaction layers in this order: fast open/focus through the authorized Browser owner; typed Browser actions for supported controls; accessible DOM refs; visual Canvas inspection and action when controls are canvas-only; browser_console scripts or synthetic events only as the final fallback. Verify visible app state after every mutation and before retrying. A canvas screenshot or dirty marker is visual evidence, not proof that a file was saved or a learning capability was compiled. Keep provider calls, tokens, and cost unknown unless the canonical owner returns them. Full worked case study (Trello): `references/trello-case-study.md`. Bulk messaging a roster through a web messenger: `references/whatsapp-web-batch-send.md`. Who compiles a repetitive batch (and why nothing will nudge you): `references/deterministic-batches-and-compilation.md`. ## 0. First prove you are in the app, not on a loading or login screen **That proof is a tool result from this session, never the request itself.** An "aberto e verificado" report written without a `browser_navigate`/snapshot/console result behind it is a fabricated observation, and it surfaces on the user's very next question ("o que você vê?"). Open, read, then report — and when the page turns out to be a canvas/WASM app whose DOM holds nothing, report *that* instead of describing a screen you never read (`js-rendered-site-extraction` § When the DOM is genuinely empty — canvas / WASM apps). A successful `browser_navigate` and a "loading… [100%]" indicator are **not** evidence of a usable session. A WhatsApp Web load reported `Carregando conversas [8%] → [35%] → [69%] → [100%]` and then settled on the **QR login screen** — zero controls to automate. Probe authoritative DOM markers in one call, and **poll** instead of sleeping a fixed time (the SPA mounts after `readyState: complete`): ```js JSON.stringify({ readyState: document.readyState, paneSide: !!document.querySelector('#pane-side'), rows: document.querySelectorAll('[role="row"][data-testid^="list-item-"]').length, qr: !!document.querySelector('canvas[aria-label], div[data-ref]'), sess: Object.keys(localStorage).filter(k => k.startsWith('wds')).length }) ``` - Decide from the **app's own chrome** (its side pane, list rows, search input) and from the app's **session keys in `localStorage`** — never from progress text or `readyState`. - A native-browser runtime is its **own profile**: the user being logged into Chrome, or into another app's browser, says nothing about this session. - `browser_snapshot` returning `element_count: 0` is **not** proof the page is empty — an SPA mid-mount looks like that. Probe by JS before concluding. **Authentication is the user's step, not yours.** You cannot log in for them; when the probe says "not logged in", stop and hand over the path that actually works remotely: - A QR rendered in the page **refreshes on a short cycle (~20s)** — a screenshot sent to the user arrives already expired. Share the screenshot only to point at which window to look at, and tell them to scan from the live window. - Prefer the app's **code-based pairing** alternative ("connect with phone number" → an 8-digit code typed on the phone): one copyable code beats a QR that changes before the user looks at it. Read the code out of the DOM and dictate it. - Leave "keep me signed in on this browser" checked when offered — otherwise the user re-pairs on every profile restart. ## 1. Know your evaluator's powers and limits `browser_console` **awaits promises** — `(async () => { ... })()` with `await` and a local `sleep` works, which is what makes UI automation viable at all. ```js const sleep = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)); ``` **It also has a controller timeout.** Three `sleep(3000)` in one call produced `WorkstationBrowserError: Hermes Browser controller request timed out`. Keep each call to **~3–4s of accumulated waiting**; split long jobs across calls and append results to a workspace file if the job is big. **A call that times out is not a mutation that failed.** `… timed out after dispatch` means the request *left* — the page-side work often completes anyway (a card description was saved by a call that reported a timeout). Read the state back before repeating anything: a blind retry of a mutation that already landed duplicates or overwrites it. **To beat the timeout on slow per-item work, stop waiting inside the page.** Kick the work off, return immediately, and poll from later calls. Chain each item onto a page-global promise and collect per-item results in a page-global array: ```js window.__done = window.__done || []; window.__q = (window.__q || Promise.resolve()).then(() => __fill(item, payload).then(r => window.__done.push(r))); 'QUEUED'; // returns in milliseconds ``` Read `window.__done.length` / `String(window.__done)` in cheap follow-up calls, and sleep in the **shell** between polls (`terminal: sleep 20`) — an in-page wait loop is subject to the same controller timeout, so it cannot be the fix. ### Call hygiene for long per-item loops Each rule below cost real round-trips when ignored. - **Pair the action call and the read call in ONE assistant turn.** A `browser_navigate` (or a `location.assign` console call) followed in the same turn by the `browser_console` read is executed in order, so a loop over N pages advances one item per turn instead of two. Have the read return `location.pathname` together with the expected identifier, so a read that arrived before the navigation is visible at once instead of being mistaken for an empty page. - **Vary the expression text between iterations of the same call.** A loop that issues a byte-identical tool call repeatedly can trip the mutation-approval gate and hand the turn to the user mid-collection. Embed the current target id (or a counter) in the expression — same effect, distinct text. The same holds for a shell command used as a timer between browser calls (`terminal: sleep 7`): a byte-identical repeat trips the gate as well, so vary its text or keep the wait inside the console call. - **Wait on a readiness token, not a clock.** Poll the page for the app's own label (`document.body.innerText.indexOf('Visualiza') >= 0 && length > 90`) in a short loop of ~450 ms steps; a fixed sleep either wastes the budget or reads a half-rendered panel. - **Keep each write-argument small when relaying page text to disk through your own tool calls.** One item (post, row, record) per file, roughly 1 KB, is the safe unit. A single oversized argument (~3 KB was enough) can arrive *truncated* and be written without any error — a silently corrupt file. Never conclude from "the write succeeded". Close the loop by parsing every file with a script and asserting the count, id uniqueness, and the presence of the expected markers before any downstream step consumes them. - **Order the fallbacks for getting data out of a page:** in-page accumulator printed in the console result (always works) → shell/clipboard bridge for actual files → a local HTTP sink. A page's CSP applies to page-side `fetch`, so an https origin posting to `http://127.0.0.1:...` is typically refused, and a page-initiated download raises a native dialog that page JS cannot dismiss. When either route stalls, stop after one probe and take the accumulator path — do not debug the transport. **Exception, verified:** CSP gates page-side `fetch` only. A **top-level navigation** to `http://127.0.0.1:/sink?n=file.txt&d=` carries the payload in the query string and is *not* subject to `connect-src` — that is the byte-exact route **out** of a page (§8), and a local page writing `window.name` before `location.replace(appUrl)` is the byte-exact route **in**. - **Keep an injected helper alive by navigating inside the app.** Load the list/board once, inject `window.__fill`, then move item to item by clicking the item's own anchor (`a[href^="/c/"]`) — an SPA transition keeps the injected globals. A top-level `browser_navigate` reloads the document and silently drops them, so every item then costs a fresh injection. - **Relaying a big payload *into* the page: compress it and make it self-checking.** gzip+base64 cuts the console argument ~3×, but the real value is that corruption cannot pass silently — `atob` throws `InvalidCharacterError` on a mangled base64 and the decompressor throws on mangled bytes, so a bad relay fails loudly instead of writing wrong text. After the write, assert the control's length/sentinel and read the server state back. - **A `handoff_requested` result is a stop, not a retry loop.** When the mutation gate fires, the call did *not* run. Short single-purpose expressions pass where long compound ones (several DOM globals in one `JSON.stringify`) trip it. Retry the same intent once with a simpler expression; if it persists, stop and ask the human to confirm the pending handoff — never route around it with another tool. **But the retry is itself what kills the confirmation:** each gated call supersedes the previous request and mints a fresh `handoff_id` (a superseded call surfaces as `CANCELLED`), so a retry loop leaves the human nothing stable to approve and never terminates — the id you just showed them is already dead. For a gated navigation there is no simpler-expression retry at all: name the live `handoff_id` and its target, end the turn, and wait for the approval. Bulk mutation raises the odds, so keep batches small and verify between them. While the gate is closed, switch to read-only work (read the app's own edit history, gather evidence, draft the plan) instead of re-issuing mutations — **navigations count as mutations** for this gate, so a retry loop of `browser_navigate` gets refused too. ### Persist confirmed items to disk, batch by batch A page-global accumulator (`window.__done`) is a **transport, not a record**: it dies with the tab, and once the mutation gate closes or the context is compacted the only list of what landed is the conversation. A long run can end with dozens of confirmed writes and no way to enumerate them. - After every batch, write the confirmed pairs (item id + status) to a file on disk **before** queueing the next batch — one line per item, append-only. - Recover the remaining work from that file plus the app's own read endpoint (`GET …?fields=desc`), never from your recollection of the conversation. - If you cannot enumerate the remaining items from disk plus one read, the run is not resumable — stop and close that gap before writing anything else. **A failed compressed relay is regenerated, not patched.** `InvalidCharacterError` from `atob`, or a decompressor fault, means the base64 was mangled *in transit* (a long argument relayed through tool calls), not that the content is wrong. Re-run the generator script to emit a fresh payload and re-queue that item; emit the payload as one line from a script and copy it verbatim — never hand-assemble or hand-repair base64. **Verified:** synchronous `XMLHttpRequest` (`x.open(method, url, false)`) works inside the page and is the most direct way to read authenticated state. ## 2. Filling inputs — match the mechanism to the control There is no single technique. Identify what the control actually *is* first (`tagName`, `contenteditable`, `role`) before writing to it. ### 2a. {"success": true, "name": "browser-console-ui-automation", "file": "references/whatsapp-web-batch-send.md", "content": "# Bulk outbound messaging through a web messenger (WhatsApp Web)

Class of task: a roster (event check-ins, contact sheet, attendee list) and one
message that every person on it must receive, individually, with proof per
recipient. Drive the **internal browser** on `https://web.whatsapp.com/`, not a
third-party messenger bridge.

## 0. Preconditions

- Session live: `#pane-side` present (a load indicator is not proof — §0 of the
  main skill).
- Read the roster and build a **control file** before sending anything:

```json
{"msg": "<literal message>",
 "items": [{"nome": "…", "empresa": "…", "phone": "5564996111840",
            "digits": 13, "url": "https://web.whatsapp.com/send?phone=…&text=…",
            "status": "pending"}]}
```

- Normalize each phone to **digits only** (strip `+`, spaces, dashes) and keep
  both the raw and the digit form. **Exclude the sender** by comparing the
  roster's own email/phone field, not by guessing from a name.
- Encode the text with `urllib.parse.quote` once and reuse the same URL.
- Never guess a missing/odd-looking number. Send only the digits the roster
  carries.

## 1. Per recipient: open → send → verify (two calls)

**Call A — open the conversation from page JS:**

```js
location.assign('https://web.whatsapp.com/send?phone=<digits>&text=<urlencoded>');
```

WhatsApp prefills the composer with the text as its **own** state, which is why
this path is trustworthy: the submit is not a synthetic insert, so the app's own
send control accepts it (contrast pitfall 15 — the trust gate only bites when
*you* wrote the text into the editor).

**Call B — wait, verify, send:**

```js
const MSG = '…';
let c; for (let i = 0; i < 8 && !(c = document.querySelector('footer [contenteditable="true"]')) || c.innerText.trim() !== MSG; i++) await sleep(400);
const chat = document.querySelector('[data-testid="conversation-info-header"]').innerText;
const btn = document.querySelector('button[aria-label="Enviar"][data-tab="11"]')
         || document.querySelector('button[aria-label="Enviar"]')
         || document.querySelector('[data-testid="send"]');
```

Click only when **both** hold: the composer text equals the message exactly, and
the chat header is the intended person. Then assert the send landed: the composer
is empty and the message is the last bubble in
`[data-testid="conversation-panel-messages"]`.

- **The first `assign` after a conversation is open frequently lands nowhere.**
  Confirm the header changed; if not, re-issue the assign once. Never assume the
  target changed because the assign returned without error.
- Each assign **replaces the document**, so the following call may still evaluate
  against the stale one (it answers with the previous person's header). Read the
  header every time and treat a mismatched header as "not ready", never as a send.
- Stale-composer safety: if the header is the previous person *and* the composer
  still holds the message, the click would re-send. The empty-composer assertion
  after every send is what makes this class of run safe.

## 2. Names will not match the roster

WhatsApp titles come from the account or the address book, not from the roster:
a check-in name may appear as a business nickname, a first name plus company, or
just the number (`+55 64 9987-1693` when unsaved). Match on the **phone you sent
to**, record the observed title next to the roster name in your report, and never
skip a recipient because the title "looks wrong".

## 3. When a number cannot receive

- WhatsApp answers an unreachable number with **"O número +… não está no
  WhatsApp"** and shows an OK dialog. Mark that item `failed_invalid`, dismiss the
  dialog (`[role="dialog"]` → the OK button), and **report the number to the
  human** — a duplicated DDD or a shifted digit is theirs to resolve. Do not
  invent a corrected number, and do not send to a best guess.
- Raw digits typed into the search box find nothing (`Nenhuma conversa, contato ou
  mensagem encontrada`) — the search box is not a phone lookup. Use the deep link.

## 4. Leave no drafts behind

Anything you injected into a composer for probing shows up in the chat list as
`Rascunho: <text>`. Clear it before finishing: open that chat, then a synthetic
`Ctrl+A` keydown followed by a synthetic `Backspace` keydown (the app's keymap
does the deletion — `paste('')` does not). Verify the word `Rascunho` is gone from
`#pane-side`.

## 5. Several messages into the SAME chat (test sends, sequences)

Do not run one fill+send per model turn: the text is literal and the target is
fixed, so emit the whole sequence as **one** awaited call and verify once.

```js
const chat = document.querySelector('#main [data-testid="conversation-info-header"]')?.innerText || '';
const count = () => document.querySelectorAll('#main [data-testid="msg-container"]').length;
const before = count();
for (const t of ['Teste 1/5', 'Teste 2/5', 'Teste 3/5']) {
  const el = document.querySelector('footer [contenteditable="true"]');
  el.focus();
  const dt = new DataTransfer();
  dt.setData('text/plain', t);
  el.dispatchEvent(new ClipboardEvent('paste', {clipboardData: dt, bubbles: true, cancelable: true}));
  await sleep(700);                       // let Lexical commit the state
  document.querySelector('button[aria-label="Enviar"]')?.click();
  await sleep(700);
}
JSON.stringify({chat, before, after: count()});
```

- **Keep the whole loop under the controller timeout** (§1): 4–5 messages fit;
  for more, queue on a page-global promise and poll.
- **Never verify a paste by re-reading the composer in a later call.** After a
  re-render the composer can read empty even though the paste landed; the retry
  then appends a second copy and the single bubble ships doubled. Fill and send
  in the same call, and count `msg-container` before/after instead.
- Before starting, confirm the header really is the intended chat (a leftover

{"code": "import csv, json, re, os, hashlib, unicodedata
base = r"C:\Users\Kevyn Lucas\Downloads\Enviar"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(open(os.path.join(base,"pessoas-acirv.csv"), encoding="utf-8-sig"), delimiter=";"))

img = os.path.join(base, "Oficina Inicia.IA Gestão.png")

    d = re.sub(r"\D","",t or "")

    return d

items=[]

    items.append({"nome": r["nome"].strip(), "empresa": (r.get("empresa") or "").strip(),
                  "phone_raw": r["telefone"].strip(), "phone": d, "digits": len(d),
                  "status": "pending", "sent_at": None, "observed_title": None, "error": None})
ctrl = {"created_at": "2026-10-19", "message": msg, "image": os.path.basename(img),
        "image_sha256": hashlib.sha256(open(img,'rb').read()).hexdigest(),
        "total": len(items), "items": items}
out = os.path.join(base, "envio_controle.json")
json.dump(ctrl, open(out,"w",encoding="utf-8"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=1)
print("controle:", out, "| itens:", len(items))
print("números 12 díg:", sum(1 for i in items if i["digits"]==12), "| 13 díg:", sum(1 for i in items if i["digits"]==13))
"}

# Inspecting the live Hermes desktop DOM

## Overview

When you are developing `apps/desktop` and the user is running that same app
(`hgui` / `npm run dev`), you can read the **live rendered DOM** of the window
they are looking at — computed styles, geometry, which CSS rule actually won,
console output — instead of inferring it from `.tsx` and being wrong.

Dev-server runs open a Chrome DevTools Protocol port on `127.0.0.1:9222`
automatically. The renderer is a Chromium page, so everything DevTools can read,
a script can read.

**This does not replace looking at it.** CDP answers *factual* questions ("what
is the computed padding", "did this element render", "which selector matches").
It cannot tell you whether the result looks good. Colour balance, spacing feel,
and "is this ugly" still need the user's eyes or a screenshot. Answer facts with
CDP; hand aesthetics to the user.

## When to Use

- Verifying a UI change actually took effect in the running app
- "Why is this element still X?" — find the winning rule before editing anything
- Locating a stable selector for a component you're about to change
- Checking a design token's computed value on a real node
- Reading renderer console errors the user mentions but can't copy out

**Don't use for:** perf profiling or heap work (`node-inspect-debugger`,
`debugging-hermes-desktop`), or anything where the real question is "does this
look right".

## The port

Open on `127.0.0.1:9222` for any dev-server run. Closed in exactly two cases
(`apps/desktop/electron/dev-cdp.ts`):

- **packaged builds** — always, and no environment value overrides it;
- **no `HERMES_DESKTOP_DEV_SERVER`** — an unpackaged `electron .` against
  `dist/` is how the packaged app gets smoke tested, so it behaves like one.

`HERMES_DESKTOP_CDP_PORT` moves the port (`=9333`) or disables it (`=off`).

Check before doing anything else:

```bash
curl -s --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:${HERMES_DESKTOP_CDP_PORT:-9222}/json/version
```

Empty → no port. Do not guess another port silently.

**Never relaunch the user's app to get a port.** That destroys their session and
their state. Launch your own isolated instance instead (below).

## Reading the DOM

`apps/desktop/scripts/eval.mjs` is the one-liner:

```bash
cd apps/desktop
node scripts/eval.mjs "document.querySelectorAll('[data-slot]').length"
```

For multi-step work use the shared client — it has target discovery and
promise-aware eval:

```js
import { CDP, SELECTORS } from './scripts/perf/lib/cdp.mjs'

const cdp = await CDP.connect({ port: 9222, match: '5174' })
const out = await cdp.eval(`JSON.stringify({
  radius: getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--radius-scalar').trim(),
  composer: !!document.querySelector('[data-slot="composer-rich-input"]')
})`)
cdp.close()
```

`SELECTORS` in `scripts/perf/lib/cdp.mjs` holds the stable `data-slot` hooks
(composer, thread viewport, assistant message, turn pair, profile rail). Prefer
them over inventing a `querySelector` — they are updated as a unit when
components move.

## The question this is best at: which rule won?

Editing every call site because a style "isn't applying" is the classic waste.
Read the real node first:

```js
const el = document.querySelector('[data-slot="aui_assistant-message-root"] a')
JSON.stringify({
  ownClasses: el.className,
  weight: getComputedStyle(el).fontWeight,
  parents: (() => {
    const out = []
    let n = el
    while ((n = n.parentElement) && out.length < 6) out.push(n.className)
    return out
  })()
})
```

If the node carries no class of its own, the value is **inherited** — sweeping
call sites will not fix it, and you need the ancestor rule. A plugin stylesheet
(e.g. `@tailwindcss/typography`'s `prose a { font-weight: 500 }`) routinely beats
a utility class; override on the shared class, not at each usage.

When there is no port, or you must not disturb the user's window:

```bash
cd apps/desktop
HERMES_HOME=$HOME/.hermes/cache/scratch/cdp-probe-home \
HERMES_DESKTOP_DEV_SERVER=http://127.0.0.1:5174 \

```

The separate `--user-data-dir` dodges Electron's single-instance lock, so it
cannot collide with a running `hgui`; the separate `HERMES_HOME` keeps it away

the background and kill it when done.

`npm run perf:serve` does the same with a temp `HERMES_HOME` baked in, if you
also want the perf harness.

- **Never kill the user's dev server or app to "free" anything.** A mid-serve

  gets blamed on whatever you just changed.

{"content": """"Handoff de dados para a pagina do WhatsApp Web via fragmento de URL. CSP de web.whatsapp.com bloqueia fetch/XHR para localhost (connect-src) e imagens (img-src), logo o unico canal de bytes e' navegacao de topo. window.name e' limpo em navegacao cross-site pelo Chrome, mas o fragmento (#) sobrevive e nao passa pelo contexto do agente. GET /go?f=[&t=] -> redireciona para # GET /ping """ import base64, os, sys from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer from urllib.parse import urlparse, parse_qs HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)) BASE = "https://web.whatsapp.com/" class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def log_message(self, *a): pass def do_GET(self): u = urlparse(self.path) q = parse_qs(u.query) if u.path == "/ping": body = b"pong" self.send_response(200) self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain") self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body))) self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(body) return if u.path != "/go" or "f" not in q: self.send_response(404); self.end_headers(); return name = os.path.basename(q["f"][0]) path = os.path.join(HERE, name) if not os.path.isfile(path): self.send_response(404); self.end_headers(); return with open(path, "rb") as fh: raw = fh.read() frag = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(raw).decode().rstrip("=") base = q.get("t", [BASE])[0] target = f"{base}#{frag}" body = f"""handoff

""".encode("utf-8") self.send_response(200) self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=utf-8") self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body))) self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(body) if __name__ == "__main__": port = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 8769 ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), H).serve_forever() ", "path": "C:\Users\Kevyn Lucas\Downloads\Enviar\handoff.py"}
